**Audience**: a student with the sheet's prerequisites — basics of machine learning and Python — who wants to learn deep learning together with its costs: the FLOPs, memory and communication of a training run or of a served model. **Empirical first**: each topic starts from a failure seen in practice — an out-of-memory error on a 7B model caused by a poor sharding choice, a speedup of only 1.2× despite 8 GPUs (Amdahl's law) — and only then names the tools that explain it: complexity bounds, data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, quantization.

The module covers the P1 foundations in cost-oriented form, then adds what the lower bounds allow and how real GPUs behave.

### What you will be able to do

-   Write, debug and monitor a complete PyTorch training pipeline for a network of several million parameters.
-   Explain automatic differentiation, universal approximation and what is (and is not) guaranteed in non-convex training.
-   Build a transformer block from the multilayer perceptron (attention, positions, pre-LN, causal mask), and choose and justify an architecture for images (CNN, with its equivariance), sequences (RNN, LSTM) and text generation (causal transformer).
-   Bound the sensitivity of a network to input perturbations, and explain adversarial examples and adversarial training.
-   State the policy gradient theorem and the principles of deep Q-learning, and count what a deep RL run costs in rollouts and memory.
-   Derive the training objectives of VAEs, GANs and diffusion models, and implement a diffusion sampler.
-   Count the FLOPs and memory of a model, and connect these counts to scaling laws.
-   Explain the theoretical complexity bounds of training and what they rule out.
-   Choose a parallelism strategy — data, tensor, pipeline — and justify it quantitatively.
-   Analyze collective communications (all-reduce and friends) and their effective cost.
-   Reduce the memory footprint of a training run with checkpointing and ZeRO.
-   Make inference efficient and know at what performance price.
-   Read a roofline and predict the behavior of a real system, from GPU to 7B LLM.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

Officially, the APM_52183_EP course unit offers an in-depth presentation of the *practical* and *theoretical* aspects of deep learning: on the one hand the mastery of Python / PyTorch implementation (implementation, debugging, visualization), on the other the analysis of foundations (automatic differentiation, universality results, non-convex optimization, equivariant models).

The stated objective is twofold: give an overview of the deep learning landscape and of its applications, in traditional fields and in new ones, and make students able to train by themselves a deep network of several million parameters, with PyTorch.

Prerequisites stated on the sheet (for the engineering degree and the exchange programmes): *basics in Machine Learning* and *coding in Python*.

The sheet lists a nine-item programme, in the order below; every item, and every theoretical topic of the description, is mapped to the section that teaches it.

### Where this course fits in the program

One of the six options of the Period 2 “Choose 1” group, and the second way to satisfy the track rule “Deep Learning required once, in P1 or P2”: a student who did not take [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) in Period 1 takes this course instead, as the AI-systems route of the home page does. It therefore assumes no earlier deep learning course.

Official prerequisites (stated for the engineering degree and the exchange programmes): *basics in Machine Learning* and *coding in Python*. In this programme they are covered by [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) (Period 1) and by chapters 2–6 of the off-curriculum [Refresher on neural networks](../m1p1-refresher-neural-nets/index.html). Chapter 0 builds everything else, from the training pipeline to the transformer block, before the cost chapters.

The other options of the same group (Optimization for AI, Multimodal Generative AI, …) cannot be taken alongside this course: the page cites their notes only as optional reading. It runs in parallel with the mandatory [Reinforcement Learning](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html), Graph ML and NLP courses, to which sections 7.2 and 7.3 and chapter 0 link.

Downstream, the module directly prepares [ML Ops and LLM Engineering Principles](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html) (M2), where these cost accounts become deployment decisions, and [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html) (M2), whose large-scale analyses build on the same scaling laws and budgets.

### Course outline

-   **Foundations: the field, the PyTorch pipeline, autodiff, optimization and the transformer block** — the tasks of deep learning, universal approximation, a complete training script with its debugging checks, automatic differentiation, optimization for deep networks with its rates, and the transformer block built from the multilayer perceptron.
-   **Counting: FLOPs, memory, scaling laws** — the module's basic discipline, quantify before asserting, applied to the architectures of the official syllabus: CNNs and equivariant models, recurrent networks, transformers for text generation.
-   **Parallelism: data, tensor, pipeline** — the three main ways of distributing a training run, and their trade-offs.
-   **Communication: all-reduce and friends** — the collectives that connect the workers, and their share of total time.
-   **Memory efficiency: checkpointing, ZeRO** — fitting models and states that do not fit.
-   **Efficient inference** — cutting the cost of the trained model at the moment it serves.
-   **Real systems: roofline, GPU, 7B LLM** — confronting theoretical accounts with hardware, on a textbook case.
-   **Stability, robustness, reinforcement learning and generative models** — Lipschitz bounds and adversarial examples, deep Q-learning and policy gradients, VAEs, GANs and diffusion.
-   **Theoretical complexity of training** — the lower bounds that say what no trick will ever beat, once the systems side is known.
-   **Research readings: lower bounds and Lipschitz regularity** — the papers of K. Scaman and co-authors behind chapter 8 and section 7.1 (not the works of the official team), read with the module's tools.
-   **Exercises** — counts, bounds and parallelism choices to defend.
-   **Projects and assessment** — solo and group subjects that measure what the course counts, a written-exam proposal and a grading rubric.
-   **References** — the systems and theory papers underlying each chapter.

### How to study this module

-   Work through chapter 0 seriously: it is the course's only foundation (no earlier deep learning course is assumed), and the cost vocabulary is introduced there.
-   Quantify everything: for every architecture encountered elsewhere, practice estimating FLOPs and memory before looking up the answer.
-   Never separate theory from hardware: a complexity bound is read facing a roofline.
-   Recompute the systems chapter's examples on paper, then check against GPU orders of magnitude.
-   Keep the rates of chapter 0 (theorem 0.10, proposition 0.11) at hand: the $\sqrt{\kappa}$ of the lower bounds of chapter 8 starts there.
-   Do the exercises by estimating first, computing second: the order of magnitude first is the target skill.

This module provides this language of budgets, common to the systems courses and the M2 LLM courses — and directly marketable in careers in large-scale ML engineering as in research on distributed learning.

## 0. Foundations: the field, the PyTorch pipeline, autodiff, optimization and the transformer block {#ch0}

This chapter lays the foundation that the rest of the module relies on, assuming only the sheet's prerequisites: basics of machine learning and Python. It covers the first three themes of the official syllabus — the field and its tasks (with the universal approximation theorem), the training pipeline in PyTorch, and optimization for deep learning, with automatic differentiation in between — and ends by building the transformer block from the multilayer perceptron.

Readers who want backpropagation worked by hand on tiny networks first can use chapters 2–6 of the off-curriculum [Refresher on neural networks](../m1p1-refresher-neural-nets/index.html).

::: note
[The pedagogical contract of the P2 variant]{.tag} This variant teaches the same official foundations as the P1 course, and asks of each one "how much does it cost, and how far can one go?". Three questions organize everything:

-   **(Q1)** *count* — predict the FLOPs and memory of a training run *before* launching it (ch. 1, 6);
-   **(Q2)** *parallelize* — decompose the compute time over several machines, and know what theory forbids (ch. 2–4, then the limits proved in ch. 8);
-   **(Q3)** *compress* — reduce the inference cost at nearly equal quality (ch. 5).

The lower bounds of ch. 8 come from the distributed-optimization literature (the papers of ch. 9): this module is the place in the master's program where one proves *lower bounds*, not just algorithms.
:::

### The field: tasks, architectures and what a network can represent {#dl-landscape}

Deep networks are the default tool for vision and language, and are spreading to the sciences. The official syllabus follows the main families of tasks; the table says where each one is treated here.

  Task                                      Data                            Typical architecture                       Section
  ----------------------------------------- ------------------------------- ------------------------------------------ --------------------------------------------
  image analysis                            pixel grids                     convolutional network (CNN)                [ch. 1, CNNs](#dl-cnn)
  regression / classification of sequences  time series, audio, sensors     recurrent network (RNN, LSTM)              [ch. 1, RNNs](#dl-rnn)
  text generation                           token sequences                 causal transformer                         [ch. 1, text generation](#dl-textgen), ch. 5
  sequential decisions                      interactions with a system      deep reinforcement learning                [section 7.2](#dl-rl)
  generating new data                       images, text, molecules         VAE, GAN, diffusion                        [section 7.3](#dl-generative)

Why should a network be able to represent the function that solves such a task? The classical answer is the universal approximation theorem.

::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Universal approximation (Cybenko 1989; Hornik 1991; Leshno, Lin, Pinkus & Schocken 1993)]{.tag} Let $\sigma\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous and not a polynomial.

For every continuous function $f$ on a compact set $K \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist a width $N$ and parameters $a_j, b_j \in \mathbb{R}$, $w_j \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that the one-hidden-layer network
$$
g(x) = \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_j\,\sigma(w_j^\top x + b_j)
$$
satisfies
$$
\sup_{x \in K}|f(x) - g(x)| \leq \varepsilon .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — An explicit ReLU construction in one dimension (proved)]{.tag} Let $f$ be $L$-Lipschitz on $[0, 1]$ and $n \geq 1$. With the knots $x_k = k/n$ and the slopes $s_k = n\big(f(x_{k+1}) - f(x_k)\big)$, the network
$$
g(x) = f(0) + s_0\,\mathrm{ReLU}(x) + \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(s_k - s_{k-1})\,\mathrm{ReLU}(x - x_k)
$$
has $n$ hidden units and satisfies
$$
\sup_{[0,1]}|f - g| \leq L/n .
$$

::: proof
On $[x_k, x_{k+1}]$ exactly the units with knots $x_0, \dots, x_k$ are active, so $g$ is affine there with slope
$$
s_0 + (s_1 - s_0) + \dots + (s_k - s_{k-1}) = s_k .
$$

Since $g(0) = f(0)$, induction on $k$ gives $g(x_k) = f(x_k)$ at every knot: $g$ is the piecewise linear interpolant of $f$.

For $x \in [x_k, x_{k+1}]$, $g(x) = \lambda f(x_k) + (1 - \lambda) f(x_{k+1})$ for some $\lambda \in [0, 1]$, hence
$$
|f(x) - g(x)| \leq \lambda|f(x) - f(x_k)| + (1-\lambda)|f(x) - f(x_{k+1})| \leq L/n ,
$$
because both distances to the knots are at most $1/n$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[What the theorem does not say]{.tag} It guarantees existence, not efficiency nor learnability. The grid construction above needs about $(L/\varepsilon)^d$ units in dimension $d$, an exponential cost; depth changes this picture, since some functions computed by deep narrow networks require exponentially many units with one hidden layer (Telgarsky 2016). Nor does it say that gradient descent will find the approximating weights: that is the question of the optimization section below.

Theorem 0.1 is admitted here. The P1 Deep Learning notes (ch. 1.2) sketch Cybenko's proof for a sigmoidal $\sigma$; the general non-polynomial case of Leshno et al. (1993), which covers ReLU, needs more analysis; proposition 0.2 proves the one-dimensional ReLU case.
:::

### The training pipeline in PyTorch {#dl-pipeline}

Every training script, from a small classifier to a large language model, is built from the same five objects: a **dataset** (indexable, returning one example and its label), a **data loader** (batching, shuffling, parallel loading), a **model** (an `nn.Module` whose parameters are registered automatically), a **loss**, and an **optimizer** that updates the parameters from their gradients. The loop alternates a training phase (forward pass, loss, backward pass, update) and an evaluation phase without gradients.

The script below trains a ResNet-18 — about $11.2$ million parameters, the order of size the official objectives ask students to master — on CIFAR-10.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
import torchvision, torchvision.transforms as T

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
norm = T.Normalize((0.49, 0.48, 0.45), (0.25, 0.24, 0.26))
train = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10("data", train=True, download=True,
    transform=T.Compose([T.RandomCrop(32, padding=4), T.RandomHorizontalFlip(), T.ToTensor(), norm]))
test = torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10("data", train=False, download=True,
    transform=T.Compose([T.ToTensor(), norm]))
train_dl = DataLoader(train, batch_size=128, shuffle=True, num_workers=4)
test_dl = DataLoader(test, batch_size=512)

model = torchvision.models.resnet18(num_classes=10).to(device)
print(sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))        # 11,181,642
epochs = 30
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1, momentum=0.9, weight_decay=5e-4)
sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.OneCycleLR(opt, max_lr=0.1, total_steps=epochs * len(train_dl))
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(epochs):
    model.train()
    for x, y in train_dl:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()                 # reverse-mode automatic differentiation
        opt.step(); sched.step()
    model.eval(); correct = 0
    with torch.no_grad():               # no graph is stored during evaluation
        for x, y in test_dl:
            correct += (model(x.to(device)).argmax(1).cpu() == y).sum().item()
    print(f"epoch {epoch}: last train loss {loss.item():.3f}, test acc {correct / len(test):.3f}")
```

::: note
[Debugging and visualization: the checks that catch most bugs]{.tag}

1.  **Initial loss**: with $K$ balanced classes and a freshly initialized network, the cross-entropy should be close to $\ln K$ ($\ln 10 \approx 2.30$ here); a very different value points to a bug in the labels, the loss or the initialization.
2.  **Overfit one batch**: training on a single batch of $32$ examples must drive the loss near $0$; if it does not, the model, the loss or the optimizer is wrong, independently of any data issue.
3.  **Look at the inputs** after augmentation and normalization, by displaying a few images with their labels.
4.  **Monitor** the training and validation curves, the learning rate and the gradient norm per layer (TensorBoard or an equivalent tool): a gradient norm that explodes precedes a divergence, a validation curve that rises while the training curve falls is overfitting.
5.  **Fix the seeds** and save checkpoints, so that a run can be reproduced and resumed.
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.3 — The first two numbers to compute before training]{.tag} For the script above:

1.  the initial loss should read about $2.30$;
2.  the training state in fp32 holds the weights ($11.2 \times 10^6 \times 4$ bytes $\approx 45$ MB), their gradients ($45$ MB) and the momentum buffer of SGD ($45$ MB): about $134$ MB, to which the activations of the current batch are added (they grow linearly with the batch size and with the image resolution).

With Adam in mixed precision, definition 1.4 below gives $16$ bytes per parameter, about $179$ MB.

The same accounting, applied to a model with $7$ billion parameters, is what ch. 1 and ch. 4 turn into sharding decisions.
:::

### Automatic differentiation: what `loss.backward()` computes {#dl-autodiff}

A network is a program made of elementary operations. Automatic differentiation computes the exact derivatives of such a program — not a finite-difference approximation, and not a symbolic formula — by applying the chain rule operation by operation.

::: def
[Definition 0.4 — Evaluation trace, forward and reverse modes]{.tag} The program computes intermediate values $v_1, \dots, v_m$, each by an elementary operation of earlier ones, $v_i = \phi_i(v_j : j \in \mathrm{pa}(i))$, the inputs being the first values and the output $y$ the last.

**Forward mode** propagates tangents
$$
\dot v_i = \sum_{j \in \mathrm{pa}(i)} \frac{\partial \phi_i}{\partial v_j}\,\dot v_j
$$
alongside the evaluation: one pass gives the derivative along *one input direction*.

**Reverse mode** first evaluates and stores the trace, then propagates adjoints backwards,
$$
\bar v_j = \sum_{i : j \in \mathrm{pa}(i)} \bar v_i\,\frac{\partial \phi_i}{\partial v_j}
$$
starting from $\bar y = 1$: one backward pass gives the derivative of the output with respect to *all inputs*.

Backpropagation is reverse mode applied to the loss.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — The cheap gradient principle (Baur–Strassen 1983; Griewank)]{.tag} For a scalar function of $p$ parameters computed by a program of elementary operations, reverse mode returns the whole gradient at a cost bounded by a small constant times the cost of one evaluation, independently of $p$; forward mode would need $p$ passes.

The reason is local: each elementary operation with $k$ arguments contributes $k$ partial derivatives, used once in the backward sweep, which is of the same order as evaluating it.

The price is memory: all the intermediate values must be stored until the backward pass, which is why activations dominate the training memory (def. 1.4) and why checkpointing (ch. 4) trades recomputation for memory.

For a dense network the constant is about $2$:
$$
\text{backward} \approx 4ND \quad \text{against} \quad \text{forward} \approx 2ND \ \text{FLOPs (theorem 1.3)}.
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 0.6 — One forward and one backward pass by hand]{.tag} Take $f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2 + \sin x_1$ at $(x_1, x_2) = (\pi, 2)$.

1.  **Forward trace:**
    $$
    v_1 = \pi, \quad v_2 = 2, \quad v_3 = v_1 v_2 = 2\pi, \quad v_4 = \sin v_1 = 0, \quad v_5 = v_3 + v_4 = 2\pi .
    $$
2.  **Backward sweep** from $\bar v_5 = 1$: $\bar v_3 = \bar v_4 = 1$; then
    $$
    \bar v_2 = \bar v_3\, v_1 = \pi \quad\text{and}\quad \bar v_1 = \bar v_3\, v_2 + \bar v_4 \cos v_1 = 2 - 1 = 1 .
    $$

Hence
$$
\nabla f(\pi, 2) = (1, \pi),
$$
which matches the formulas $\partial_1 f = x_2 + \cos x_1$ and $\partial_2 f = x_1$.

In PyTorch, `x = torch.tensor([math.pi, 2.0], requires_grad=True); (x[0]*x[1] + torch.sin(x[0])).backward()` leaves exactly $(1, \pi)$ in `x.grad`.
:::

### Optimization for deep learning {#dl-optim}

Training minimizes the empirical risk $F(\theta) = \frac1n\sum_i \ell(h_\theta(x_i), y_i)$, which is non-convex as soon as there is a hidden layer.

Two algorithms do almost all the work. The first is SGD with momentum, where $g_k$ is the mini-batch gradient at step $k$:
$$
m_{k+1} = \beta m_k + g_k, \qquad \theta_{k+1} = \theta_k - \eta\, m_{k+1}.
$$
The second is Adam/AdamW (definition 0.9 below), which divides each coordinate of the step by a running estimate of the gradient's magnitude. Three facts specific to deep networks decide whether they work: initialization, the learning rate, and clipping.

::::: prop
[Proposition 0.7 — Initialization that preserves the signal (He et al. 2015, proved)]{.tag} Consider a layer $z = W x$ with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ whose entries are independent, centred, of variance $s^2$, independent of the input $x = \mathrm{ReLU}(u)$, where the coordinates of $u$ are centred, symmetric and identically distributed. Then

::: key
[Key result — variance propagation through a ReLU layer]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{Var}(z_i) = \frac{n s^2}{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(u_j).
$$
:::

The choice $s^2 = 2/n$ (He initialization) keeps the variance of the pre-activations constant from layer to layer; a smaller $s^2$ makes it vanish geometrically with depth, a larger one makes it explode.

::: proof
$z_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} W_{ij} x_j$ is a sum of $n$ independent centred terms, so
$$
\mathrm{Var}(z_i) = \sum_j \mathbb{E}[W_{ij}^2]\,\mathbb{E}[x_j^2] = n s^2\, \mathbb{E}[x_j^2].
$$

Since $u_j$ is symmetric, $\mathrm{ReLU}(u_j)^2$ equals $u_j^2$ on half of the distribution and $0$ on the other half, so
$$
\mathbb{E}[x_j^2] = \tfrac12\mathbb{E}[u_j^2] = \tfrac12\mathrm{Var}(u_j).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
:::::

::: ex
[Example 0.8 — The learning rate that diverges]{.tag} On $f(\theta) = \tfrac{L}{2}\theta^2$, gradient descent gives $\theta_{k+1} = (1 - \eta L)\theta_k$: it converges if and only if
$$
\eta < 2/L .
$$

For a network, the role of the curvature $L$ is played by the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian of the loss (the *sharpness*), which is unknown and changes during training.

Hence the practical recipe: find the largest learning rate that does not diverge on a short run, use a fraction of it, start with a **warmup** (a linear ramp over the first percent of the steps, while the early curvature is high and Adam's moment estimates are poor), then **decay** it (cosine or steps).

**Gradient clipping**, $g \mapsto g\min(1, c/\|g\|)$, caps the damage of a rare large gradient.
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.9 — Adam and AdamW (Kingma & Ba 2015; Loshchilov & Hutter 2019)]{.tag} Adam keeps two states per parameter, started at $m_0 = v_0 = 0$.

Its hyperparameters are the learning rate $\eta$, the decay rates $\beta_1, \beta_2$ (defaults 0.9 and 0.999), a small $\varepsilon$ and the weight decay $\lambda$. At each step $k \geq 1$, coordinate by coordinate:
$$
m_k = \beta_1 m_{k-1} + (1-\beta_1)\, g_k, \qquad v_k = \beta_2 v_{k-1} + (1-\beta_2)\, g_k^2,
$$
$$
\hat m_k = \frac{m_k}{1-\beta_1^k}, \qquad \hat v_k = \frac{v_k}{1-\beta_2^k}, \qquad \theta_k = \theta_{k-1} - \eta\Big(\frac{\hat m_k}{\sqrt{\hat v_k} + \varepsilon} + \lambda\,\theta_{k-1}\Big).
$$

The bias corrections undo the start from zero.

**AdamW** applies the decay $\lambda\theta$ outside the adaptive ratio, as written. Plain Adam with “L2 regularization” adds $\lambda\theta$ to $g_k$ instead: the decay is then divided by $\sqrt{\hat v_k}$, and the weights with large gradients are barely regularized.

The two states $m, v$ are the 8 bytes per parameter of the training-memory table of ch. 1 (definition 1.4).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.10 — SGD on a non-convex objective (Ghadimi & Lan 2013, proved)]{.tag} Let $F$ be $L$-smooth (its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz) and bounded below by $F^\star$, and let $\Delta = F(\theta_0) - F^\star$.

Assume the stochastic gradients $g_k$ are unbiased with variance at most $\sigma^2$. SGD with the constant step
$$
\eta = \min\Big(\frac1L,\ \sqrt{\frac{2\Delta}{L\sigma^2 K}}\Big)
$$
satisfies, after $K$ steps,
$$
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \mathbb{E}\,\|\nabla F(\theta_k)\|^2 \;\leq\; \frac{4L\Delta}{K} + 2\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2L\Delta}{K}}.
$$

The guarantee is a small gradient on average: a near-stationary point, at the rate $O(1/\sqrt K)$ with gradient noise and $O(1/K)$ without.

::: proof
The descent lemma of $L$-smooth functions, with $\eta \leq 1/L$ and the variance bound
$$
\mathbb{E}\|g_k\|^2 \leq \|\nabla F(\theta_k)\|^2 + \sigma^2 ,
$$
gives
$$
\mathbb{E}\,F(\theta_{k+1}) \leq \mathbb{E}\,F(\theta_k) - \frac{\eta}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(\theta_k)\|^2 + \frac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}{2}.
$$

Summing over $k < K$ and using $F \geq F^\star$:
$$
\frac1K\sum_{k<K}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(\theta_k)\|^2 \leq \frac{2\Delta}{\eta K} + L\eta\sigma^2 .
$$

If $\eta$ is the square root, both terms equal $\sigma\sqrt{2L\Delta/K}$. If $\eta = 1/L$, then $\sigma^2 \leq 2L\Delta/K$ and the sum is at most $4L\Delta/K$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.11 — Gradient descent versus Nesterov acceleration (Nesterov 1983, 2004; stated)]{.tag} Let $f$ be $L$-smooth and $\mu$-strongly convex, with condition number $\kappa = L/\mu$.

-   Gradient descent with step $1/L$ needs $O(\kappa\ln(1/\varepsilon))$ gradient evaluations to reach accuracy $\varepsilon$ (theorem 0.5 of the [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html#gd-sgd) course, proved there for quadratics, next to the convex SGD rate).
-   Nesterov's accelerated gradient needs only $O(\sqrt{\kappa}\ln(1/\varepsilon))$:
    $$
    y_k = x_k + \frac{\sqrt\kappa - 1}{\sqrt\kappa + 1}\,(x_k - x_{k-1}), \qquad x_{k+1} = y_k - \frac1L\nabla f(y_k).
    $$
-   No method that only combines gradients does better on all such functions (Nesterov 2004, ch. 2).

For $\kappa = 10^4$: about $10^4\ln(1/\varepsilon)$ steps against $100\ln(1/\varepsilon)$. Chapter 8 meets the same $\sqrt\kappa$ in distributed training, multiplied by a network factor.
:::

::: note
[Non-convex optimization: what is guaranteed, what is observed]{.tag} The guarantee is modest: with a step tuned to the horizon, SGD reaches points whose average squared gradient norm is $O(1/\sqrt{K})$ after $K$ steps (theorem 0.10) — stationary points, not minima.

What is observed is much better, for three reasons studied in research:

-   in high dimension, most critical points with a high loss are saddle points rather than poor local minima (Dauphin et al. 2014), and the noise of SGD helps to escape them (Ge et al. 2015);
-   overparameterized networks have many connected near-global minima;
-   normalization layers and residual connections (next section) keep the landscape well conditioned along the trajectory.
:::

### From MLP to transformer block {#dl-transformer}

The cost chapters count convolutional networks and transformers. This section builds both from the multilayer perceptron, so that the module needs no earlier deep learning course.

Shapes follow the site convention. A linear layer is $h = Wx + b$ with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\mathrm{out} \times d_\mathrm{in}}$ (the `weight` of `nn.Linear`). A sequence of $n$ tokens of width $d$ is a matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, one token per row.

**Convolution: output size and receptive field.** A convolutional layer replaces the dense matrix by a small $k \times k$ filter slid over the image; ch. 1 writes it out (definition 1.7) and counts its cost. With padding $p$ and stride $s$, an input of side $H$ gives an output of side
$$
H' = \Big\lfloor \frac{H + 2p - k}{s} \Big\rfloor + 1 .
$$

For a 32-pixel input, a 3×3 filter and padding 1, the output keeps side 32 with stride 1 (the “same” padding of the ResNet-18 above) and halves to 16 with stride 2.

Each output of a stack of $L$ such layers with stride $1$ sees a patch of side $1 + L(k-1)$ of the input, its *receptive field*: it grows linearly with depth, and faster with strides or pooling.

**Attention.** In a convolution each position mixes a fixed neighbourhood; in attention each token decides, from the data, which other tokens to read.

::: def
[Definition 0.12 — Scaled dot-product and multi-head attention (Vaswani et al. 2017)]{.tag} One attention *head* projects the tokens into queries, keys and values,
$$
Q = XW_Q, \qquad K = XW_K, \qquad V = XW_V, \qquad W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_k},
$$
and returns
$$
\mathrm{Att}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\Big)V ,
$$
the softmax acting on each row. Row $i$ of the output is an average of the value vectors, weighted by how well query $i$ matches each key.

**Multi-head attention** runs $h$ heads with $d_k = d/h$ in parallel, concatenates their outputs into an $n \times d$ matrix and multiplies it by $W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.13 — Why divide by $\sqrt{d_k}$ (proved)]{.tag} Let the coordinates of a query $q$ and a key $k$ be independent, centred and of variance $1$.

Then the score $q^\top k$ has mean $0$ and variance $d_k$, and the scaled score $q^\top k/\sqrt{d_k}$ has variance $1$, whatever the head width.

::: proof
$q^\top k = \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} q_j k_j$ is a sum of $d_k$ independent centred terms, each of variance
$$
\mathbb{E}[q_j^2 k_j^2] = \mathbb{E}[q_j^2]\,\mathbb{E}[k_j^2] = 1 .
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Without the scaling, at $d_k = 64$ the scores have standard deviation $8$. A softmax of such spread-out scores is nearly one-hot, and its Jacobian $\mathrm{diag}(p) - pp^\top$ is then nearly zero: gradients stop flowing through the head. The scaling plays the role that He initialization (prop. 0.7) plays for linear layers.

**Positions.** Attention alone ignores order: permuting the rows of $X$ permutes the rows of the output in the same way (permutation equivariance, the symmetry studied in ch. 1, definition 1.10). Order is injected by adding a position vector $p_i$ to the embedding of token $i$:

-   *learned* positions: one trained vector per position, as in GPT-2;
-   *sinusoidal* positions (Vaswani et al. 2017):
    $$
    p_{i,2j} = \sin\big(i/10000^{2j/d}\big), \qquad p_{i,2j+1} = \cos\big(i/10000^{2j/d}\big),
    $$
    whose fixed frequencies make $p_{i+\Delta}$ a rotation of $p_i$, hence an easy function of relative position.

Recent LLMs rotate the queries and keys instead of adding vectors (RoPE, see the [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch2) course).

**Tokens: byte-pair encoding in five lines** (Sennrich et al. 2016).

1.  Start from single bytes.
2.  Count the adjacent pairs of symbols in a training corpus.
3.  Merge the most frequent pair into a new symbol, and record the merge.
4.  Repeat until the vocabulary reaches its target size ($50\,257$ tokens for GPT-2).
5.  Encode new text by replaying the merges in order.

Frequent words become one token, rare words split into pieces, and no word is ever out of vocabulary. Variants and their trade-offs: [Text Mining and NLP](../m1p2-nlp-text-mining/index.html#ch1), ch. 1.

::: def
[Definition 0.14 — Pre-LN transformer block with causal mask]{.tag} With $\mathrm{LN}$ the layer normalization of each token (zero mean, unit variance, then a learned scale and shift), a block maps $X$ to
$$
H = X + \mathrm{MHA}\big(\mathrm{LN}(X)\big), \qquad Y = H + \mathrm{MLP}\big(\mathrm{LN}(H)\big),
$$
where $\mathrm{MLP}(u) = W_2\,\mathrm{GELU}(W_1 u)$ acts on each token, with $W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{4d \times d}$ and $W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times 4d}$.

For generation, token $i$ may only read tokens $j \leq i$. The **causal mask** $M$, with $M_{ij} = 0$ if $j \leq i$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, is added before the softmax:
$$
\mathrm{softmax}\Big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\Big)V .
$$

Row $i$ of the output then depends on $x_1, \dots, x_i$ only.
:::

*Residual connections* make each sublayer a correction to the identity. The gradient reaches the first layers through the sums, without crossing every block's Jacobian, so the product of prop. 1.13 (the vanishing gradient of recurrent networks) never forms.

*Pre-LN* (normalizing before each sublayer, from GPT-2 on) keeps that identity path clean; the original post-LN design needed a long warmup to train at all (Xiong et al. 2020).

The block below is a complete, runnable version; ch. 1 counts its parameters ($12d^2$ plus biases) and its FLOPs.

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class Block(nn.Module):                      # pre-LN transformer block, causal
    def __init__(self, d=768, h=12):
        super().__init__()
        self.h, self.ln1, self.ln2 = h, nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.qkv, self.proj = nn.Linear(d, 3 * d), nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.mlp = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4 * d, d))

    def forward(self, x):                     # x: (batch, n, d)
        b, n, d = x.shape
        q, k, v = self.qkv(self.ln1(x)).view(b, n, 3, self.h, d // self.h).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)
        mask = torch.ones(n, n, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device).tril()
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (d // self.h) ** 0.5      # (b, h, n, n) scores
        att = att.masked_fill(~mask, float("-inf")).softmax(-1)
        x = x + self.proj((att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(b, n, d))
        return x + self.mlp(self.ln2(x))

print(sum(p.numel() for p in Block().parameters()))   # 7,087,872 = 12 d^2 + 13 d
```

**LoRA in five lines** (Hu et al. 2022). Fine-tuning all the weights costs the full 16 bytes per parameter of ch. 1 (definition 1.4). LoRA freezes each pretrained matrix $W_0$, of size $d_\mathrm{out} \times d_\mathrm{in}$, and learns a low-rank correction:
$$
W = W_0 + BA, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\mathrm{out} \times r}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_\mathrm{in}}, \quad r \ll \min(d_\mathrm{in}, d_\mathrm{out}) .
$$

$B$ starts at zero, so training starts from the pretrained model. Only $r(d_\mathrm{in} + d_\mathrm{out})$ parameters per matrix receive gradients and Adam states. After training, $BA$ is added into $W_0$, so inference costs nothing extra.

For $d_\mathrm{in} = d_\mathrm{out} = 4096$ and $r = 8$: $65\,536$ trainable parameters instead of $16.8$ M per matrix, $256$ times fewer.

## 1. Counting: FLOPs, memory, scaling laws {#ch1}

A GPU budget is easily burned because nobody counted the FLOPs and the bytes before launching the job. This chapter teaches the module's first skill, **exact counting**: predicting the compute and the memory of a training run from the architecture alone.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three confusions cost the most: mixing up a FLOP count and a FLOP/s throughput, forgetting that memory bandwidth (not compute) often sets the speed, and adding GPUs without checking what Amdahl's law allows.
:::

The point of counting by hand: An engineer who can estimate the FLOPs of a training run by hand saves GPU-days — and catches configuration errors before they explode.

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Units: FLOP, FLOPs, FLOP/s]{.tag} A **FLOP** (floating-point operation) = one elementary operation (+, ×); we count a multiply-add $a \cdot b + c$ as **2 FLOPs** (the module's convention, aligned with the systems literature); **FLOP/s** = throughput.

An A100 GPU: ≈ 19.5 TFLOP/s fp32, 312 TFLOP/s tensor-core bf16; an H100: ≈ 1000 TFLOP/s bf16 (sparse modes excluded).

The **MFU** (model FLOPs utilization) = achieved FLOP/s ÷ peak FLOP/s: 35–50% is a good LLM training run; the rest is lost to memory, communication and subtasks (ch. 6).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Cost of a linear layer and a transformer (proved)]{.tag}

-   **(i)** A matrix-matrix product $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ by $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ costs $2mnp$ FLOPs.
-   **(ii)** A linear layer $d_\mathrm{in} \to d_\mathrm{out}$ applied to $n$ tokens costs $2\,n\,d_\mathrm{in}d_\mathrm{out}$ FLOPs and has $d_\mathrm{in}d_\mathrm{out}$ parameters — that is, **2 FLOPs per parameter and per token**.
-   **(iii)** Transformer block of width $d$, over a sequence of $n$ tokens:
    -   QKVO $4 \times 2d^2 = 8d^2$,
    -   scores $QK^\top$ and product with $V$: $2 \times 2n^2 d$,
    -   MLP (width $4d$): $2 \times 2 \times 4d^2 = 16d^2$

    — that is, *per token*:
    $$
    24d^2 + 4nd \ \text{FLOPs}.
    $$

::: proof
-   **(i)** Each of the $mp$ entries of $C=AB$ is a dot product of length $n$ (n multiplications + n−1 additions ≈ 2n FLOPs).
-   **(ii)** special case with $m=n$ tokens, $p = d_\mathrm{out}$.
-   **(iii)** apply (ii) to each projection; for $QK^\top$ (an $n \times d$ by $d \times n$ matrix):
    $$
    2n^2 d,
    $$
    likewise for $(\cdot)V$ ($n \times n$ by $n \times d$).

    MLP = two layers $d \to 4d$ then $4d \to d$.

    Divide the total by $n$ tokens to express it per token: QKV projections ($3 \times 2d^2$) + output ($2d^2$) = $8d^2$, quadratic part of attention $4nd$, MLP $16d^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — The rule $C \approx 6\,N\,D$ (proved)]{.tag} Pre-training a model with $N$ parameters (dense transformer) on $D$ tokens costs

::: key
[Key result — the training-compute rule]{.tag}
$$
C \;\approx\; 6\,N\,D \;\;\text{FLOPs} \qquad (\text{forward} \approx 2ND,\; \text{backward} \approx 4ND).
$$
:::

::: proof
Forward pass: the model is a composition of linear layers and negligible operations (normalizations, softmax: $O(nd)$ or $O(n^2)$ without a $d^2$ factor); each parameter is used exactly once per token, at 2 FLOPs each (prop. 1.2 ii) — hence $2ND$.

Backward pass: for each layer, the gradient is computed by

-   **(a)** applying the transpose of the weight to the upstream gradient ($2ND$) and
-   **(b)** multiplying the upstream gradient by the local input to form the weight gradient ($2ND$)

— that is $2 \times 2ND$. Total $6ND$.

Experience (profiling of large training runs) confirms within ±10%, the gap coming from (shared) embeddings, the vocabulary and the heads. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 1.4 — Training memory, line by line (Adam, mixed precision)]{.tag} For $N$ parameters:

  Tensor                                                         Precision   Bytes/parameter
  -------------------------------------------------------------- ----------- -------------------------------------------
  weights (bf16/fp16)                                            2 bytes     2
  gradients (bf16)                                               2           2
  Adam states $m, v$ (fp32)                                      4 + 4       8
  fp32 master weights (stability)                                4           4
  **total states**                                                           **16**
  activations (depend on $n, d$, number of layers) — see ch. 4   2           about $34\,d$ per token and per layer

The activation line follows Korthikanti et al. (2022): a transformer layer keeps about $34\,d$ bytes per token in bf16, plus a term that grows with the context length when the attention scores are stored.

Order of magnitude to remember: **16 bytes per parameter** of states + activations. A 7B model with Adam: $7\times10^9 \times 16$ ≈ 112 GB — before any activation: a single 80 GB GPU is not enough (ch. 4 and 6).
:::

::: note
[The GPU memory hierarchy, in one box]{.tag} A GPU computes in its streaming multiprocessors, each with registers and a small on-chip SRAM: 192 KB per multiprocessor on an A100, about 20 MB in all, read at roughly 19 TB/s. Behind them sit a 40 MB L2 cache and the HBM, the “GPU memory” of `nvidia-smi`: 80 GB at about 2 TB/s (figures of Dao et al. 2022).

Beyond the card, NVLink joins the GPUs of a node (600 GB/s per A100), InfiniBand joins nodes (about 25 GB/s per link) and PCIe reaches the host memory (about 32 GB/s). Each step down is several to tens of times slower, and much larger. Every count of this module — the 16 bytes per parameter, the KV cache, the all-reduce, the roofline of ch. 6 — asks at which level the bytes live and how often they cross a boundary.
:::

::: note
[Scaling laws: from Kaplan to Chinchilla (the budget as a primary dimension)]{.tag} **Kaplan et al. 2020**: over decades, the loss follows a power law
$$
L(N, D) \approx (N_c/N)^{\alpha_N} + (D_c/D)^{\alpha_D} + L_\infty
$$
— first reading: enlarging the model helps more than enlarging the data.

**Hoffmann et al. 2022 (Chinchilla)**: with the compute budget $C = 6ND$ *fixed*, the optimum is reached for $D \approx 20 N$ — the models of the Kaplan era were *undertrained*; GPT-3 (300B tokens for 175B parameters) was "too big" for its data, and Chinchilla — 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens (example 1.6), trained with the budget of the 280B Gopher — outperforms both.

Method lesson for this module: the budget $C$ is not a side constraint, it is the axis along which one *designs* the model.

(The M2 LLMs module, ch. 3, revisits these laws in detail; the "energy" angle is in the Optimization and Responsible AI for Sustainability module, ch. 6.)
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.5 — Counting GPT-2 small by hand]{.tag} GPT-2 small has $12$ blocks of width $d = 768$, a context of $n = 1024$ tokens and a vocabulary of $50\,257$ tokens.

1.  *Parameters.* A block holds $4d^2$ (attention projections) $+ 8d^2$ (MLP) $= 12d^2 \approx 7.1$M parameters, so the $12$ blocks hold about $85$M.

    The token embeddings add $50\,257 \times 768 \approx 38.6$M, which gives the announced $124$M once position embeddings and biases are included.
2.  *FLOPs per token, forward.* By prop. 1.2, a block costs
    $$
    24d^2 + 4nd \approx 14.2\text{M} + 3.1\text{M} \approx 17.3\text{M FLOPs},
    $$
    i.e. about $208$M for the $12$ blocks; the output layer (logits over the vocabulary) adds $2 \times 768 \times 50\,257 \approx 77$M.

The attention term $4nd$ equals $24d^2$ when $n = 6d$: below a context of about $4\,600$ tokens for this width, the matrix products dominate and the rule "2 FLOPs per parameter and per token" is accurate; for long contexts, the quadratic term takes over.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.6 — Sizing a model from a compute budget with the Chinchilla rule]{.tag} With a budget of $C = 10^{23}$ FLOPs and the ratio $D \approx 20N$, the rule $C = 6ND$ becomes $C = 120\,N^2$, so
$$
N = \sqrt{C/120} \approx 2.9 \times 10^{10} \ \text{parameters} \quad\text{and}\quad D \approx 5.8 \times 10^{11} \ \text{tokens}:
$$
a model of about $29$B parameters trained on about $580$B tokens.

As a check, Chinchilla itself ($70$B parameters, $1.4$T tokens) corresponds to
$$
6 \times 7 \times 10^{10} \times 1.4 \times 10^{12} \approx 5.9 \times 10^{23} \ \text{FLOPs},
$$
with $D/N = 20$.

Halving the budget divides $N$ and $D$ by $\sqrt 2$ each, not $N$ alone by two.
:::

```python
def flops_transformer(N_params, D_tokens, fwd_ratio=2.0, bwd_ratio=4.0):
    return (fwd_ratio + bwd_ratio) * N_params * D_tokens

C = flops_transformer(6.7e9, 1e12)                  # LLaMA-7B ~ 6.7B params, 1T tokens
print(f"{C:.2e} FLOPs")                              # 4.02e22
peak, mfu = 312e12, 0.45                             # A100 bf16, 45% MFU
hours = C / (peak * mfu) / 3600
print(f"{hours:,.0f} GPU-hours")                     # ~80,000 -- see ch. 6 and Touvron et al. 2023
```

### Image analysis: convolutional networks {#dl-cnn}

Images are large (a $224 \times 224$ colour image has $150\,528$ values) and their content does not depend on where an object sits. Convolutional networks exploit both facts: each output looks only at a small neighbourhood (locality), and the same filter is applied at every position (weight sharing).

::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Convolutional layer]{.tag} For an input $X \in \mathbb{R}^{c_\mathrm{in} \times H \times W}$ and a kernel
$$
K \in \mathbb{R}^{c_\mathrm{out} \times c_\mathrm{in} \times k \times k},
$$
the layer computes (stride $1$, zero padding) $$Y_{o,i,j} = b_o + \sum_{c=1}^{c_\mathrm{in}}\sum_{u,v=0}^{k-1} K_{o,c,u,v}\, X_{c,\,i+u,\,j+v}.$$

It has $c_\mathrm{out}c_\mathrm{in}k^2 + c_\mathrm{out}$ parameters and costs $2\,H'W'\,c_\mathrm{out}c_\mathrm{in}k^2$ FLOPs for an $H' \times W'$ output — prop. 1.2 (ii) with $H'W'$ positions playing the role of tokens.

A network stacks such layers with non-linearities and downsampling (stride or pooling); classification ends with a global average pooling and a linear layer, detection predicts boxes and classes at many positions, segmentation predicts a label per pixel with an encoder-decoder (U-Net).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Convolution commutes with translations (proved)]{.tag} Let $(\tau_t X)_{c,i,j} = X_{c,\,i - t_1,\,j - t_2}$ translate an image by $t = (t_1, t_2)$ (on an infinite grid, or away from the borders). Then
$$
\mathrm{conv}(\tau_t X) = \tau_t\,\mathrm{conv}(X):
$$
the layer is translation-equivariant, and a global pooling after it makes the network translation-invariant.

::: proof
$$
\mathrm{conv}(\tau_t X)_{o,i,j} = b_o + \sum_{c,u,v} K_{o,c,u,v}\, X_{c,\,i - t_1 + u,\,j - t_2 + v} = \mathrm{conv}(X)_{o,\,i - t_1,\,j - t_2} = \big(\tau_t\,\mathrm{conv}(X)\big)_{o,i,j},
$$
since the same kernel is used at every position.

Pointwise non-linearities commute with translations too, so the whole stack is equivariant; a global average sums over all positions and forgets the shift. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.9 — What weight sharing saves]{.tag} A $3 \times 3$ convolution from $64$ to $64$ channels on a $56 \times 56$ map (a ResNet stage) has $64 \times 64 \times 9 = 36\,864$ weights and costs
$$
2 \times 56^2 \times 64 \times 64 \times 9 \approx 0.23 \ \text{GFLOPs}.
$$

A dense layer between the same input and output, each of size $64 \times 56^2 = 200\,704$, would have $200\,704^2 \approx 4 \times 10^{10}$ weights: locality and sharing divide the parameter count by about $10^6$.

The compute, on the other hand, stays large, because the small kernel is applied at every one of the $3\,136$ positions: CNNs are compute-bound, which is why they map well onto GPUs (ch. 6).

*The same count for a vision transformer* (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021). ViT-B/16 cuts a $224 \times 224$ image into $196$ patches of $16 \times 16$ pixels, plus one class token: $n = 197$ tokens of width $d = 768$, through $12$ blocks. By prop. 1.2 (iii), one image costs
$$
12 \times 197 \times (24d^2 + 4nd) \approx 3.5 \times 10^{10} \ \text{FLOPs}
$$
in the forward pass, about $35$ GFLOPs — the “17.5 GFLOPs” of vision papers, which count a multiply-add once.
:::

### Equivariant models {#dl-equivariant}

Proposition 1.8 is one instance of a general design principle: when the task is unchanged by a group of transformations of the input, build that symmetry into the architecture instead of learning it from augmented data.

::: def
[Definition 1.10 — Equivariance and invariance]{.tag} Let a group $G$ act on the inputs by $x \mapsto \rho_\mathrm{in}(g)x$ and on the outputs by $y \mapsto \rho_\mathrm{out}(g)y$. A map $f$ is **$G$-equivariant** if
$$
f(\rho_\mathrm{in}(g)x) = \rho_\mathrm{out}(g)f(x) \quad \text{for all } g \in G \text{ and all } x,
$$
and **$G$-invariant** if $f(\rho_\mathrm{in}(g)x) = f(x)$.

Examples: translations of an image and convolutional networks; permutations of the elements of a set and DeepSets, graph neural networks or self-attention without positional encoding; rotations of the plane and group-equivariant CNNs (Cohen & Welling 2016); rotations of the sphere and spherical models used for weather and climate, such as the spherical Fourier neural operators of Bonev et al. (2023).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.11 — Permutation-equivariant linear layers (Zaheer et al. 2017, proved)]{.tag} A linear map $W\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ satisfies $WP = PW$ for every permutation matrix $P$ if and only if
$$
W = a I + b\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top
$$
for two scalars $a, b$. An equivariant layer on sets of $n$ scalars therefore has $2$ parameters instead of $n^2$, whatever $n$.

::: proof
$WP = PW$ for the permutation $\pi$ means $W_{\pi(i)\pi(j)} = W_{ij}$ for all $i, j$.

Any index $i$ can be sent to any $i'$ by a permutation, so all diagonal entries are equal, to $a + b$ say.

Any ordered pair of distinct indices $(i, j)$ can be sent to any other such pair $(i', j')$, so all off-diagonal entries are equal, to $b$. Hence $W = aI + b\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top$.

Conversely $IP = PI$ and
$$
\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top P = \mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top = P\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top,
$$
because every row and column of $P$ sums to $1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The layer $x \mapsto ax + b(\mathbf{1}^\top x)\mathbf{1}$ processes each element ($ax_i$) and adds a summary of the whole set ($b\sum_j x_j$): it is the skeleton of DeepSets and of message passing on graphs. Built-in symmetry gives the right behaviour on every input, not only on those seen with augmentation, and it saves parameters and data.

### Sequential data: recurrent networks {#dl-rnn}

Time series, audio and sensor streams have a variable length and an order. A recurrent network reads them one step at a time and carries a state that summarizes the past; it can output a single prediction for the whole sequence (classification) or one prediction per step (regression, forecasting).

::: def
[Definition 1.12 — Recurrent network and backpropagation through time]{.tag} With input $x_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d_\mathrm{in}}$ and state $h_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$: $$h_t = \tanh(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b), \qquad \hat y_t = V h_t, \qquad t = 1, \dots, n.$$

The same parameters $(W, U, b, V)$ are used at every step. Training unrolls the recursion into a deep network of depth $n$, the sequence length, and applies backpropagation to it (*backpropagation through time*).

Each step costs about $2(d^2 + d\,d_\mathrm{in})$ FLOPs, but step $t$ needs $h_{t-1}$: the $n$ steps cannot be computed in parallel, unlike the $n$ positions of a transformer (prop. 1.2).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.13 — Vanishing and exploding gradients (proved)]{.tag} With $a_s = W h_{s-1} + U x_s + b$, $$\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial h_t} = \prod_{s=t+1}^{n} \mathrm{diag}\big(\tanh'(a_s)\big)\,W, \qquad \Big\|\frac{\partial h_n}{\partial h_t}\Big\| \leq \|W\|^{n-t}.$$

If $\|W\| < 1$, the influence of step $t$ on the loss at step $n$ decays exponentially with the gap $n - t$; if $W$ has an eigenvalue of modulus larger than $1$ and the units stay in their linear regime, it can grow exponentially.

::: proof
The chain rule gives
$$
\partial h_s/\partial h_{s-1} = \mathrm{diag}(\tanh'(a_s))\,W,
$$
and the Jacobians multiply along the chain $h_t \to h_{t+1} \to \dots \to h_n$. The norm of a product is at most the product of the norms, and $\|\mathrm{diag}(\tanh'(a_s))\| \leq 1$ since $0 < \tanh' \leq 1$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.14 — Fifty steps of memory, and the LSTM fix]{.tag} With $\|W\| = 0.9$, a dependency $50$ steps back is weighted by at most
$$
0.9^{50} \approx 0.005 :
$$
the network cannot learn it.

The LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997) adds a cell state updated additively,
$$
c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde c_t ,
$$
where the gates $f_t, i_t \in (0,1)^d$ are computed from $x_t$ and $h_{t-1}$. Along this direct path, $\partial c_t/\partial c_{t-1} = \mathrm{diag}(f_t)$: when the forget gate stays close to $1$, the gradient crosses many steps almost intact, and the network learns how long to remember.

Exploding gradients are handled separately, by gradient clipping. The GRU is a lighter variant with two gates.
:::

### Text generation with transformers {#dl-textgen}

A language model assigns a probability to every sequence of tokens and generates text by sampling from it one token at a time. The transformer of prop. 1.2 becomes a generator through two changes: a causal mask, and a decoding rule.

::: def
[Definition 1.15 — Causal language model, teacher forcing, perplexity]{.tag} The model factorizes
$$
p_\theta(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}).
$$

In each attention layer the scores $q_t^\top k_j$ with $j > t$ are set to $-\infty$ before the softmax (**causal mask**), so that position $t$ only sees the past.

Training minimizes the cross-entropy $-\frac1n\sum_t \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})$ on real text, with the true previous tokens as inputs (**teacher forcing**): a single forward pass produces the $n$ predictions in parallel, which is what makes transformers much faster to train than RNNs.

The **perplexity**
$$
\exp\big(-\frac1n\sum_t\log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})\big)
$$
is the effective number of choices per token; a uniform model over a vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ has perplexity $|\mathcal{V}|$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.16 — Decoding: temperature, top-$k$, nucleus]{.tag} At each step the model outputs logits $z$ and the next token is drawn from $\mathrm{softmax}(z/T)$. For three candidate tokens with logits $(2, 1, 0)$:

-   at $T = 1$ the probabilities are $(0.665, 0.245, 0.090)$;
-   at $T = 0.5$ they become $(0.867, 0.117, 0.016)$, sharper;
-   at $T = 2$, $(0.506, 0.307, 0.186)$, flatter.

$T \to 0$ is greedy decoding (always the most likely token), which tends to produce repetitive text.

**Top-$k$** sampling keeps only the $k$ most likely tokens.

**Nucleus** (top-$p$) sampling keeps the smallest set whose probabilities sum to at least $p$, e.g. $p = 0.9$ keeps the first two tokens here at $T = 1$ ($0.665 + 0.245 = 0.91$), renormalized (Holtzman et al. 2020).

Generating each new token costs one forward pass for the new position only, provided the keys and values of the past are kept: this is the KV cache whose size governs inference in ch. 5 (def. 5.1).
:::

## 2. Parallelism: data, tensor, pipeline {#ch2}

This chapter answers a practical question: how to split one training run over many GPUs. There are three axes, often combined (the "3D parallelism" of large systems); for each, we give the principle, the decomposition of the time per step and the communication cost.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Data parallelism (DP)]{.tag} Each GPU holds a *complete* copy of the model, processes a different mini-batch ($B/P$ examples), then the gradients are averaged by an **all-reduce** (ch. 3).

Time per step (batch size $B$, forward+backward time $\tau_\mathrm{calc}(B)$, gradient of size $S$ bytes):
$$
T_\mathrm{DP} \;=\; \underbrace{\tau_\mathrm{calc}(B/P)}_{\text{compute, divided by } P} \;+\; \underbrace{2\,(P-1)\,\alpha + \tfrac{2(P-1)}{P}\tfrac{S}{b}}_{\text{ring all-reduce (theorem 3.2)}}.
$$

*Strong* scalability (at fixed $B$): the compute term shrinks, the communication term grows — the balance point defines the effective batch size; hence increasing $B$ with the step (LARS, You et al. 2017).

This is the default mode of PyTorch DDP.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Tensor parallelism (TP — Megatron, Shoeybi et al. 2019)]{.tag} One splits the *matrices* of the model. For the MLP block $Y = \sigma(XW_1)\,W_2$, the matrix $W_1$ is split by columns and $W_2$ by rows.

GPU $i$ holds $W_1^{[i]}$ and $W_2^{[i]}$, computes $\sigma(XW_1^{[i]})$ without any communication (the nonlinearity acts entry by entry, so column blocks stay independent), then the partial product $\sigma(XW_1^{[i]})\,W_2^{[i]}$; a single **all-reduce** sums the partial products into
$$
Y = \sum_i \sigma(XW_1^{[i]})\,W_2^{[i]}.
$$

This column-then-row split costs one all-reduce in the forward pass and one in the backward pass per block; attention is split *per head* in the same way.

TP lives on the fastest links (intra-node NVLink): every layer pays a communication — this is the "mandatory high bandwidth" parallelism.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Pipeline parallelism: the bubble (proved)]{.tag} $p$ stages (consecutive layers on each GPU), $m$ micro-batches, each micro-batch costs $\tau$ per stage. Under "1F1B" scheduling (one forward pass, one backward pass, staggered), the total time is
$$
T_\mathrm{pipe} \;=\; (m + p - 1)\,\tau, \qquad \eta \;=\; \frac{m}{m + p - 1} \;\xrightarrow[m \to \infty]{}\; 1,
$$
where $\eta$ is the efficiency; the "bubble" (stage idle time) accounts for $\frac{p-1}{m+p-1}$ of the total.

::: proof
-   **Fill-up:** the first micro-batch crosses the $p$ stages in $p\,\tau$ (stage $j$ starts at $j\tau$); afterwards each following micro-batch exits every $\tau$ units (the stages work staggered): the $m$-th exits at
    $$
    (p + m - 1)\tau .
    $$
-   **Ideal work** (without bubble): each stage processes $m$ micro-batches, i.e. $m\tau$ busy; efficiency is the ratio $m\tau / (m+p-1)\tau$.
-   **Idle time:** each stage stays idle for $(p-1)\tau$ in total (fill-up and drain combined), i.e. a fraction $(p-1)/(m+p-1)$ of the total time. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

  Mode           What is split                                  Communication                                    Required hardware                        Typical use
  -------------- ---------------------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------ ---------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------
  DP (2.1)       the batch                                      1 gradient all-reduce per step                   decent inter-node network (InfiniBand)   default, up to hundreds of GPUs
  TP (2.2)       the matrices                                   all-reduce at *every layer* (forward+backward)   intra-node NVLink (8 GPUs)               very wide models (≥ 30B), or huge width
  PP (2.3)       the layers                                     point-to-point activations between stages        any network, bubble to amortize          depth; combined with DP/TP ("3D")
  ZeRO (ch. 4)   the *states* (optimizer, gradients, weights)   like DP (all-reduce) + on-the-fly gathers        same as DP                               replacing TP when memory, not compute, is the blocker

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — When does the gradient all-reduce start to hurt?]{.tag} Train a $1$B-parameter model with data parallelism, bf16 gradients ($S = 2$ GB) and a global batch of $0.5$M tokens per step. By theorem 1.3, a step costs
$$
6 \times 10^9 \times 5 \times 10^5 = 3 \times 10^{15} \ \text{FLOPs}.
$$

-   *One node, $P = 8$ GPUs on NVLink* (say $b = 100$ GB/s per GPU for the collective): at $312$ TFLOP/s and $45\%$ MFU, compute takes
    $$
    3 \times 10^{15}/(8 \times 1.4 \times 10^{14}) \approx 2.7 \ \text{s},
    $$
    while the bandwidth term of the ring all-reduce is $\frac{2 \times 7}{8} \times \frac{2}{100} \approx 0.035$ s: about $1\%$ of the step.
-   *Sixty-four GPUs over a slower inter-node network* ($b = 25$ GB/s): compute drops to $0.33$ s, while communication grows to
    $$
    \frac{2 \times 63}{64} \times \frac{2}{25} \approx 0.16 \ \text{s},
    $$
    almost half of the compute.

Without overlapping communication and computation (ch. 3), the scaling from $8$ to $64$ GPUs would deliver a speedup of about $5.5$ instead of $8$.
:::

::: note
[Choosing: the practitioner's decision tree]{.tag}

1.  Does the model fit on one GPU with activations? → DP, end of story.
2.  The Adam states do not fit → ZeRO-2/3 (ch. 4), not TP: less communication.
3.  The weights alone do not fit ($2N$ bytes > memory) → TP intra-node (8 NVLink GPUs) + PP inter-node + DP on top; tune $m$ ≥ 4$p$ to keep the bubble under 20% (theorem 2.3).
4.  Always measure the MFU (ch. 1): below 35%, the hierarchy is poorly chosen.
:::

## 3. Communication: all-reduce and friends {#ch3}

This chapter studies the operation that connects the workers. The real bottleneck of distributed training is rarely compute: it is the **exchange of gradients**. One collective operation must be known in depth — the all-reduce — and two ways of implementing it, one that saves bandwidth and one that saves latency.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — All-reduce]{.tag} $P$ machines each hold a vector $g_i$ of $S$ bytes; all must receive $\bar g = \frac1P\sum_i g_i$ (the gradient average in DP). Homogeneous network: latency $\alpha$ per message, bandwidth $b$ bytes/s.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Ring all-reduce: bandwidth-optimal (proved)]{.tag} Arranging the $P$ machines in a ring and cutting the vector into $P$ chunks of $S/P$ bytes, the all-reduce proceeds in two phases (reduce-scatter then all-gather) of $P-1$ steps each:

::: key
[Key result — cost of the ring all-reduce]{.tag}
$$
T_\mathrm{ring} \;=\; 2\,(P-1)\,\alpha \;+\; \frac{2(P-1)}{P}\cdot\frac{S}{b} \;\xrightarrow[P \to \infty]{}\; 2\alpha P + \frac{2S}{b}.
$$
:::

The *bandwidth* term becomes independent of $P$: each machine sends $2S(P-1)/P < 2S$ bytes in total, whatever the number of machines.

This is optimal: Patarasuk and Yuan (2009) show that any all-reduce algorithm must make some machine send at least $2S(P-1)/P$ bytes.

::: proof
*Reduce-scatter.* At step $t$, machine $i$ sends a chunk (already partially summed) to $i+1$ and receives from $i-1$ a different chunk which it adds to its own.

After $P-1$ steps, machine $i$ holds the *complete* sum of chunk $i$ — each machine has sent $(P-1)\cdot S/P$ bytes.

*All-gather.* Same round in broadcast direction: the complete sums circulate, $(P-1)\cdot S/P$ bytes sent per machine.

Total per machine: $2(P-1)S/P$ bytes at rate $b$, that is $2(P-1)S/(Pb)$ — and the critical path is indeed the sequence of $2(P-1)$ steps of latency $\alpha$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.3 — Tree all-reduce: latency-optimal]{.tag} In a binary tree: reduction in $\log_2 P$ steps then broadcast in $\log_2 P$ steps, but each step transmits the *entire* vector:
$$
T_\mathrm{tree} = 2\log_2 P\,(\alpha + S/b).
$$

For small $S$ (short gradients, many small tensors): the tree wins (latency); for large $S$ (LLM gradients): the ring wins (bandwidth). Real libraries (NCCL) choose dynamically — and compose partial rings over the actual topology (intra NVLink, inter IB).
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.4 — Ring or tree, in numbers]{.tag} Take $P = 64$ machines, a latency $\alpha = 2\,\mu$s and a bandwidth $b = 25$ GB/s.

-   For a small message, $S = 64$ KB ($S/b \approx 2.6\,\mu$s): the ring costs
    $$
    2 \times 63 \times 2 + \frac{2 \times 63}{64} \times 2.6 \approx 257\,\mu\text{s},
    $$
    dominated by its $126$ latencies, while the tree costs $2 \times 6 \times (2 + 2.6) \approx 55\,\mu$s: the tree is almost five times faster.
-   For a full gradient, $S = 1$ GB ($S/b = 40$ ms): the ring costs about $0.25$ ms $+ 78.8$ ms $\approx 79$ ms, while the tree costs $12 \times 40 \approx 480$ ms: the ring is six times faster.

This is why gradients are grouped into large buckets before being reduced: a few large ring all-reduces are much cheaper than many small ones.
:::

::: note
[Three wars against the communication term: overlap, bucketing, compression]{.tag}

-   **Overlap**: while the GPU computes layer $k+1$, the gradient of layer $k$ is already on the network (async by buckets); provided $T_\mathrm{comm} \leq T_\mathrm{calc}$, communication disappears from the critical path — the raison d'être of PyTorch DDP's "bucketing".
-   **Gradient compression**: quantizing the gradients (8 bits, even 1 bit) before exchange divides $S$ by 2–16; *error feedback* (compensating the quantization error at the next step) preserves convergence — at the price of a delicate variance/theory trade-off (see the Emerging ML module, ch. 2–3 for the federated case, where communication is the limiting factor).
-   **Locality**: reducing the number of communications (local steps, gossip) is exactly the strategy dictated by the bound of ch. 8: fewer rounds, but more steps — the optimum of Scaman et al. is a precise point on this frontier.
:::

## 4. Memory efficiency: checkpointing, ZeRO, mixed precision {#ch4}

The 16 bytes per parameter of ch. 1 and the activations rarely fit on one GPU. This chapter presents three ways of trading a little computation or communication for a lot of memory: recomputing activations, partitioning the training states, and storing numbers on fewer bits.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Activation checkpointing: $O(\sqrt{L})$ memory (proved)]{.tag} A network of depth $L$, activations $a$ bytes per layer (per token/batch):

-   **(i)** without precautions, the backward pass requires $M_\mathrm{full} = L\,a$ bytes of activations;
-   **(ii)** by storing only the inputs of a partition into $\sqrt{L}$ segments of $\sqrt{L}$ layers and recomputing each segment during the backward pass (gradient checkpointing, Chen et al. 2016):
    $$
    M_\mathrm{ckpt} \;\approx\; 2\sqrt{L}\,a \;+\; O(a), \qquad \text{additional cost} \approx +\tfrac{1}{3}\ \text{of time (one extra forward pass per segment).}
    $$

::: proof
*Memory.* We store $\sqrt L$ boundary activations; during the backward pass of a segment, we replay its local forward: at most $\sqrt L$ simultaneous activations *inside* the segment (which can itself be recursively checkpointed: the memory/time trade-off can be tuned over the whole range $[a, La]$, see the $\sqrt{L}$ "compass"). Total $\sqrt L + \sqrt L = 2\sqrt L$ live activations.

*Time.* Each layer is recomputed exactly once more in the forward direction: the forward pass accounts for $1/3$ of the total cost (theorem 1.3: 2ND vs 6ND), hence about +33%. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2020): partitioning the states]{.tag} Instead of replicating the training states on every GPU (classical DP: $16N$ bytes *per GPU*), ZeRO *partitions* them:

  Stage    What is partitioned                  Memory/GPU (states)   Communication
  -------- ------------------------------------ --------------------- -------------------------------------
  ZeRO-1   Adam states ($m, v$, masters): 12N   $4N + 12N/P$          = DP
  ZeRO-2   \+ gradients ($2N$)                  $2N + 14N/P$          = DP
  ZeRO-3   \+ weights ($2N$)                    $16N/P$               ≈ 1.5 × DP (on-the-fly gathers)

Example: a 7B model on 8 GPUs. ZeRO-3 brings its $16 \times 7 = 112$ GB of states down to
$$
112/8 = 14 \ \text{GB per GPU}
$$
— the model becomes trainable on a single node, without TP or pipeline bubble (ch. 2); DeepSpeed/FSDP implement exactly this continuum.
:::

::: note
[Mixed precision: the "free" compression]{.tag} Computing in bf16 (2 bytes) instead of fp32 (4): half the memory and (on tensor cores) 2–8× the throughput; fp32 is kept for accumulators and master weights (long sums and small updates; historical fp16 additionally required *loss scaling*, Micikevicius et al. 2018).

Theorem 1.3 remains valid: we count FLOPs, precision changes the price of a FLOP. *Integer* quantization (int8/int4) only serves *inference* — ch. 5; its error analysis is proved in the notes of the Optimization and Responsible AI for Sustainability course (prop. 3.3, second part):
$$
\text{error} \leq \sum_\ell \frac{\Delta_\ell}{2}\prod_{m>\ell}\mathrm{Lip}_m .
$$
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.3 — Why the master weights stay in fp32]{.tag} The bf16 format keeps the $8$ exponent bits of fp32 — the same range, up to about $3.4 \times 10^{38}$ — but only $7$ mantissa bits, i.e. two to three significant decimal digits; fp16 has $10$ mantissa bits but only $5$ exponent bits, hence a maximum of $65\,504$ and the need for loss scaling.

Near $1$, consecutive bf16 numbers are $2^{-7} \approx 0.0078$ apart. An Adam update of $10^{-4}$ applied to a weight equal to $1$ is therefore rounded away: $1 + 10^{-4}$ is stored as $1$, and a training run in pure bf16 would simply stop learning for that weight.

Keeping an fp32 copy of the weights (spacing $2^{-23} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7}$ near $1$) lets these small updates accumulate; the bf16 copy is only used for the matrix products.
:::

::: note
[Common mistakes with training memory]{.tag}

1.  Budgeting the activations for the global batch: they scale with the *micro-batch* processed at once by each GPU, which is why gradient accumulation (several micro-batches before one optimizer step) fits large batches in small memories.
2.  Treating ZeRO-3 as free: every forward and backward pass gathers the weights on the fly, and the ZeRO paper puts its communication volume at about $1.5$ times that of plain data parallelism — acceptable on NVLink, painful on a slow network.
3.  Reading the "allocated" memory of the profiler as the peak: temporary buffers of the collectives and allocator fragmentation add to it, so a plan that fills $100\%$ of the memory on paper will fail; keep a margin.
:::

## 5. Efficient inference {#ch5}

At scale (millions of requests), inference dominates the total cost: it deserves its own tools. Four levers, from the simplest to the deepest.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — The memory-bandwidth wall of autoregressive inference]{.tag} Generating one token requires *rereading all the weights* (2N bytes in bf16) and the **KV cache** — the keys/values of past layers, to be kept for attention:
$$
\text{KV cache} \;=\; 2\;(\text{K and V})\times n_\mathrm{layers}\times n_\mathrm{ctx}\times d_\mathrm{model}\times 2\ \text{bytes} \;=\; 4\,n_\mathrm{layers}\,n_\mathrm{ctx}\,d_\mathrm{model}\ \text{bytes (bf16)}.
$$

For 7B (32 layers, $d = 4096$, context 2048):
$$
4 \times 32 \times 2048 \times 4096 \approx 1.1 \ \text{GB}
$$
— more than some believe, and *growing with the context*.

Peak throughput (one GPU, memory bandwidth $B_\mathrm{mem}$):
$$
\text{tokens/s} \;\lesssim\; \frac{B_\mathrm{mem}}{2N\ \text{bytes}} \qquad (\text{e.g. } 2\,\text{TB/s} \div 14\,\text{GB} \approx 140\ \text{tok/s}).
$$

This ceiling — and not FLOPs — governs token-by-token generation (ch. 6, roofline); batching fills the compute units without moving the wall.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — PTQ/QAT quantization, pruning, distillation (compact map)]{.tag}

| Lever | Idea | Memory/speed effect | Ref. / cross-reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| int8/int4 PTQ | round the trained weights, calibration only | 2–8× memory, up to 4× CPU/latency | Jacob et al. 2018; error bounds: Responsible AI module, ch. 3 |
| QAT | simulate rounding *during* training (STE) | int8 nearly lossless, int4 on large models | Jacob et al. 2018 |
| Structured pruning | remove whole heads/channels/layers | *effective* speedup (unlike unstructured) | Han et al. 2016 |
| Distillation | student trained on the teacher's logits softened by a temperature $T$ | 10–50× fewer parameters at similar quality on a narrow target task (the range of the Responsible AI notes, ch. 3); less on broad benchmarks: DistilBERT keeps 97 % of BERT's GLUE score with 40 % fewer parameters | Hinton et al. 2015; Sanh et al. 2019; Responsible AI notes, ch. 3 (full lab) |
| Speculative decoding | small model proposes, large model verifies *in parallel* — same distribution in theory | 2–3× tokens/s without loss | Leviathan et al. 2023 |
| IO-aware attention | rewrite attention for the GPU memory hierarchy (tiling, kernel fusion) | 2–4× training/inference on long contexts, $O(n)$ memory | Dao et al. 2022 (FlashAttention); memory hierarchy in ch. 1, roofline reading in ch. 6; see also the P1 Deep Learning notes, ch. 6.3 |
:::

::: note
[Prefill and decode: two regimes in one request]{.tag} Serving a request has two phases.

The *prefill* processes the whole prompt at once: all its tokens go through each weight matrix together, the arithmetic intensity is high and the phase is compute-bound, like training.

The *decode* then produces the answer one token at a time and is memory-bound (def. 5.1). A benchmark that reports a single "tokens per second" mixes the two and says little; report the time to first token (prefill) and the time per output token (decode) separately.

Memory also scales with concurrency: with the KV cache of def. 5.1, $32$ simultaneous sequences of $2\,048$ tokens on the 7B model need about $32 \times 1.1 \approx 35$ GB of cache in addition to the $13.4$ GB of weights — the KV cache, not the model, is what limits the batch size of an inference server.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — How many tokens does speculative decoding buy?]{.tag} A small draft model proposes $\gamma$ tokens; the large model checks them all in one parallel pass and accepts each one, in order, with probability $\alpha$ (the rejection rule of Leviathan et al. keeps the output distribution exactly that of the large model). Under the simplifying assumption that acceptances are independent, the expected number of tokens produced per pass of the large model is
$$
\mathbb{E}[\text{tokens}] = 1 + \alpha + \alpha^2 + \cdots + \alpha^{\gamma} = \frac{1 - \alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1 - \alpha},
$$
since the $j$-th proposed token is kept only if the $j-1$ previous ones were, and the pass always yields one token from the large model at the first rejection (or after the last acceptance).

With $\alpha = 0.8$ and $\gamma = 4$:
$$
(1 - 0.8^5)/0.2 \approx 3.4 \ \text{tokens per pass}.
$$

Because generation is memory-bound (def. 5.1), checking four tokens costs almost the same time as generating one, so the speedup approaches $3.4$ minus the cost of the draft model — consistent with the $2$–$3\times$ of the table.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.4 — Comparing honestly: the module's protocol]{.tag} Any compression claim is verified in four columns:

1.  *quality metric* (perplexity/accuracy — not "it feels better");
2.  *latency* at p50 and p99 (tail latency pays for cache misses);
3.  *throughput* (aggregate tokens/s);
4.  *energy per request* (J/request — Optimization and Responsible AI for Sustainability module, ch. 6).

An improvement on three columns with the fourth constant is a result; on a single one, it is a communication angle.
:::

## 6. Real systems: roofline, GPU, and the complete budget of a 7B LLM {#ch6}

This chapter confronts the counts of the previous chapters with real hardware. It explains why a GPU rarely reaches its peak throughput, bounds the speedup of any parallelization, and ends with the complete budget of a 7B model.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Roofline model (why a "312 TFLOP/s" GPU delivers 45%)]{.tag} An operation has an **arithmetic intensity** $I = \mathrm{FLOPs}/\mathrm{bytes\ read+written}$. The achievable throughput is

::: key
[Key result — the roofline]{.tag}
$$
P_\mathrm{achievable} \;=\; \min\big(P_\mathrm{peak},\; B_\mathrm{mem}\cdot I\big)
$$
:::

with $P_\mathrm{peak}$ the compute throughput and $B_\mathrm{mem}$ the memory bandwidth.

A huge GEMM (large $I$): compute-bound; an activation, a normalization, a tokenizer, token-by-token generation (low $I$): *memory*-bound — increasing the GPU's FLOP/s changes nothing there.

The 35–50% MFU of LLM training largely reflects the time spent in memory-bound operations and in communication; FlashAttention (prop. 5.2) wins by *reducing bytes*, not FLOPs — a pure roofline move.
:::

::: ex
[Example 6.2 — Reading the roofline of an A100]{.tag} With $P_\mathrm{peak} = 312$ TFLOP/s and $B_\mathrm{mem} = 2$ TB/s, the two regimes meet at the *ridge point*
$$
I^\star = 312/2 = 156 \ \text{FLOP per byte}.
$$

A product of two $n \times n$ matrices in bf16 performs $2n^3$ FLOPs and moves at least $3 \times 2n^2$ bytes, so $I = n/3$: it is compute-bound as soon as $n \gtrsim 470$.

Generating one token with batch size $1$ multiplies each weight matrix by a single vector: $2$ FLOPs per weight read, i.e. $I \approx 1$ FLOP per byte in bf16, and the achievable throughput is $B_\mathrm{mem} \cdot I \approx 2$ TFLOP/s — less than $1\%$ of the peak.

With a batch of $B$ sequences, each weight read serves $B$ tokens and $I \approx B$: decoding becomes compute-bound only around $B \approx 150$, which is why inference servers batch requests aggressively.
:::

:::: thm
[Proposition 6.3 — Amdahl's law (proved) — the ceiling of all parallelism]{.tag} If a fraction $s$ of the work is sequential (inevitably so), the speedup on $P$ processors is capped: $$A(P) \;=\; \frac{1}{s + (1-s)/P} \;\leq\; \frac{1}{s}.$$

::: proof
Sequential time $T_1 = T_s + T_p$ with $s = T_s/T_1$. On $P$ processors, the parallel part divides at best by $P$: $T_P = T_s + T_p/P$, hence
$$
A(P) = T_1/T_P = 1/(s + (1-s)/P),
$$
increasing in $P$ and bounded above by $1/s$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 6.4 — Complete case study: training a "7B" LLM (end-to-end computation)]{.tag} Assumptions (close to Touvron et al. 2023): $N = 6.7\times10^9$ parameters, $D = 10^{12}$ tokens, A100-80GB bf16 (312 TFLOP/s peak, 2 TB/s HBM, 400 W), one node = 8 GPUs + NVLink.

| Question | Computation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Total FLOPs | $6ND = 6 \times 6.7\times10^9 \times 10^{12}$ | $4.0\times10^{22}$ FLOPs |
| GPU-hours (45% MFU) | $4\times10^{22} / (312\times10^{12}\times0.45) / 3600$ | ≈ 79,000 GPU·h — the paper announces 82,432: the $6ND$ rule is accurate to ±5% |
| States memory | $16\,N = 16 \times 6.7\times10^9$ | 107 GB > 80 GB: ZeRO-2/3 or TP required (ch. 2, 4) |
| Activations (checkpointing, batch 4×2048 tokens) | $\approx 2\sqrt{32}\times(\text{layer act.})$ | a few GB/GPU: checkpointing (th. 4.1) makes the batch viable |
| Time on 256 GPUs (32 nodes) | 79,000/256 h | ≈ 13 days — hence the vital importance of MFU (half the time = 6 days saved) |
| GPU-only energy | 79,000 h × 0.4 kW (+ PUE, see the Responsible AI module, ch. 6) | ≈ 32 MWh before PUE; emissions by region: 1.6 t (FR) to \~15 t (world average) |
| fp16 inference | weights $2N$ = 13.4 GB; KV cache 2048 ctx ≈ 1.1 GB (def. 5.1) | fits on 1 80 GB GPU; throughput ≈ 140–150 tok/s (memory wall) |

This table — reused in exercise 7 — is the module's typical deliverable: a quantified budget, every line traceable to a theorem of the course (1.3, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1), and an engineer's conclusion (where to invest the next euro: MFU? memory? quantization?).
:::

::: note
[The system's keyboard: what to know about a GPU]{.tag} Memory hierarchy (registers → SRAM \~20 MB → HBM \~80 GB → NVLink → IB, the box of ch. 1); each level \~10× slower.

Winning kernels are those that maximize locality (tiling, fusion — FlashAttention again); "tensor cores" do bf16 GEMMs in 16×16×16 blocks — hence the importance of dimensions that are multiples of powers of 2, and why padding genuinely wastes.

For the ML engineer: profile *before* optimizing (nsight, PyTorch profiler), look at the roofline's "memory bound" line, and remember that the best code optimizer is a better algorithm (ch. 5).
:::

## 7. Stability, robustness, reinforcement learning and generative models {#ch7}

The previous chapters trained networks for supervised tasks and counted what that costs. This chapter covers the last three themes of the official syllabus: how stable a trained network is under small changes of its input, how deep networks learn to act from rewards instead of labels, and how they learn to generate new data. Each section gives the founding objects and one result proved in full; the specialised modules of the programme go further.

### 7.1. Stability and robustness {#dl-robust}

Stability has two meanings. *Training stability* — signals that neither vanish nor explode through depth or time — was treated with initialization (prop. 0.7), the recurrent case (prop. 1.13), normalization, residual connections and clipping. *Robustness* asks whether the trained model keeps its prediction when the input is perturbed: by an adversary who chooses a tiny worst-case perturbation, or by a shift between training and deployment data.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Lipschitz constant, adversarial example]{.tag} A map $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz (for a norm $\|\cdot\|$) if
$$
\|f(x) - f(x')\| \leq L\|x - x'\| \quad \text{for all } x, x';
$$
the smallest such $L$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(f)$.

An **adversarial example** for a classifier at $x$ is a point $x + \delta$ with $\|\delta\| \leq \epsilon$ (an imperceptible budget, e.g. $\epsilon = 8/255$ per pixel in $\ell_\infty$) that receives a different prediction.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 7.2 — Lipschitz bound of a network, certified radius (proved)]{.tag}

-   **(i)** For $f = f_L \circ \dots \circ f_1$ with $f_l(x) = \sigma(W_l x + b_l)$ and $\sigma$ $1$-Lipschitz (ReLU, tanh),
    $$
    \mathrm{Lip}_2(f) \leq \prod_{l=1}^{L}\|W_l\|_2,
    $$
    the product of the spectral norms.
-   **(ii)** If a binary classifier predicts $\mathrm{sign}\,f(x)$ with $f$ $L$-Lipschitz in $\ell_2$, every perturbation with
    $$
